data.name: Runaway, A Road Adventure
data.detailed_description:
New York, 2000...
...Without knowing how or why, Brian, a student on the verge of graduating from college, is attacked by Mafia gangsters.
During his desperate getaway, in the company of a mysterious striptease dancer, he ends up meeting a wide range of unusual characters. But which ones are trying to help him and which ones are planning to blow his head off?
You will have to be very ingenious to figure it out, without forgetting that nobody is who they seem in this explosive mixture of murder, money, ambition, santeria rituals and deception...a whole lot of deception.
  • Approximately 100 settings that are visually rich, containing 30 interactive characters.
  • Characters with soft edges, real-time lighting and shading effects, camera changes, panoramic shots and more.
  • High-quality stereo sound, an original soundtrack with over 24 songs.
  • 3D characters with a cartoon look and high-impact visual features that include 2D and 3D in an unmatchable style.

reviews.review:
*Runaway* is one of those games where I realized far too late just how terrible it actually is. I can name exactly one thing the game does well: the backgrounds for the individual scenes (excluding, of course, the dreadful 3D-animated characters) which were drawn with great detail and care.

But aside from that? Phew... 
Let’s start with the plot, which is far-fetched and dreadfully clichéd. A guy hits a good-looking woman with his car and then helps her; simply because she’s good-looking. That’s the only reason. He even says as much, out loud, to the camera. Charming, right? He stumbles from one disastrous situation to the next- which wouldn’t be so bad if he were at least somewhat interesting (I’m not even asking for him to be likable). But this guy is just incredibly unlikable. He murders, steals, and lies whenever he can, for no apparent reason.
His sidekick, Gina? She stumbles from one "damsel in distress" scenario to the next (sometimes she’s being kidnapped, other times she’s falling into caves) constantly in need of help and begging our protagonist to take her along and like her. Meanwhile, in every single scene, she wears a different outfit that presents her in a highly sexualized way.

The 3D-animated characters do not blend well with the 2D look of the background, and the dreadfully long, banal cutscenes ( which cannot be skipped or shortened are an ordeal.
Then there’s a whole range of NPCs) all of them eccentric, completely over-the-top, and rather garish. None of them have any depth, and many only appear briefly, but I suppose they’re still passably okay. The game's voice acting (in English) is pretty decent.

But the worst part is the game’s puzzles, which not only require you to meticulously scan the screen for blurry pixels, but are also completely illogical. Examples:

1) In one cutscene, a secret is revealed—a mystery that has been a central focus for much of the game. We arrive in an old area, one we’ve already spent a great deal of time exploring, with no real objective other than to figure out what the object given to us by another character actually is.
And THEN, the game expects you to use a specific mechanic in a location that had already been completely solved—tinkering with a "steam lock"—just so that, somehow, a sheriff’s star pops out?!

Example 2, right at the beginning of the game: We’re in the hospital, standing next to Gina’s bed while she sleeps. We know that some gangsters are after her, but our protagonist is convinced that she’s just exaggerating and having nightmares.
The game expects us not only to climb into the neighboring room for no apparent reason (maneuvering along a thin balustrade outside a 10th-story window) but also to search a pitch-black room for items, all to... do what, exactly? It’s never made clear; in the end, we just set everything on fire and roust Gina out of bed. Nothing is explained here, even simple storylines have to be guessed, and I  needed a guide right at the start just to figure out what the game’s objective was.

Another aspect often overlooked in other reviews is the overt racism present in this game. At certain points, the player encounters the Hopi(an Indigenous people of the Americas) who are portrayed as eccentric, delusional, mystical shamans on the verge of extinction. In reality, however, the Hopi people are very much alive and thriving in the United States; they are not "delusional" at all, but simply ordinary human beings.

Sexism, Racism, Illogical puzzles and clichés: the game offers a fine selection of terrible themes.

To top it off, the game crashed 20 minutes before the end; since there are no autosaves, I would have had to replay the entire final chapter, so I opted to watch a YouTube video instead.

Please do not buy this game, it’s not just ugly on the outside, but on the inside, too.
